text: For most of recorded history, people slept twice. Four hours, an hour awake in the dark, then four hours more.
attrib: The hour between was for thinking
caption:
Early modern England called them the first sleep and the second sleep. The waking hour between wasn't insomnia — it was ordinary, and people used it to think, read by candlelight, or talk. Street lighting is what ended it. By the 1920s the words had left the language.

text: You don't fall asleep when you get tired. You fall asleep when you get cold.
attrib: Core temperature drops about 1°C before sleep
caption:
Sleep onset lines up with the steepest part of the evening drop in core body temperature — roughly four to five hours before it bottoms out. It's one reason a cool room reads to the body as permission.

text: Ten to twenty minutes to fall asleep is the healthy range. Falling asleep instantly is a symptom, not a talent.
caption:
People treat sleep latency as a score where lower is better. It isn't. Dropping off the second your head lands usually means you were running a deficit.

text: A dolphin sleeps with half its brain at a time. One eye closes. The other half keeps watch, and keeps breathing.
caption:
Each hemisphere takes about four hours a day. For an animal that has to surface to breathe, sleeping all at once was never an option.

text: A wild giraffe sleeps about thirty minutes a day, taken in bouts of one to three minutes at a time.
caption:
The same animal in a zoo, with nothing hunting it, will sleep for hours. Sleep is as long as safety allows.

text: Great frigatebirds sleep while flying. At sea, they manage about forty-two minutes a day, in bursts of a few seconds.
attrib: On land, the same bird sleeps twelve hours
caption:
Researchers put EEG loggers on frigatebirds over the Pacific and found them sleeping mid-flight, sometimes with one hemisphere, sometimes with both.

text: Your internal clock doesn't run on twenty-four hours. Left alone in the dark, it drifts to about twenty-four and a quarter.
attrib: Morning light resets it, every day
caption:
The body clock is slightly too slow for the planet it lives on. Light in the first hour of your day is the correction.

text: The clock that runs your entire day is about twenty thousand neurons, in a piece of brain the size of a grain of rice.
caption:
Two small clusters above the crossing of the optic nerves. They take one input above all others — light — and from it set body temperature, hormone timing, alertness, and sleep.

text: The mare in nightmare is not a horse. It was a creature believed to sit on the sleeper's chest.
caption:
The word predates any explanation of sleep paralysis by about a thousand years. People described the sensation accurately long before anyone could say what it was.

text: Curfew comes from couvre-feu — cover the fire. It was not a law about being outdoors. It was the signal to bank the hearth and sleep.
caption:
A bell rang, the embers were covered, and the town went dark together. Bedtime used to be a public event.

text: Before alarm clocks, British towns employed knocker-uppers: people paid to tap your window with a long pole until you woke.
caption:
The obvious question was asked at the time, and has a dull answer: they were simply people who slept in shifts.

text: Wild elephants sleep about two hours a night, and often skip sleeping altogether for a day or more.
caption:
Among land mammals, the largest bodies tend to sleep the least. The smallest — bats, at nearly twenty hours — sleep the most.

text: Sperm whales sleep standing up, nose to the surface, drifting in silent vertical rows.
attrib: About seven percent of the day
caption:
A research boat once drifted into a pod of sleeping whales without being noticed at all — they only woke when the hull touched one.

getlullable.com

text: Jellyfish sleep. They have no brain to sleep with, which suggests sleep is older than thinking.
caption:
Upside-down jellyfish pulse more slowly at night, respond more sluggishly, and are groggy the next day if kept awake. Every animal anyone has looked at closely turns out to do some version of this.

text: Sea otters sleep holding hands, so the current doesn't carry them away from each other.
attrib: Or wrapped in kelp, for the same reason
caption:
Sleep in a moving world requires an anchor. Otters use each other.

text: A horse can doze standing up, but it has to lie down to dream. REM requires the muscles to let go.
caption:
Ligaments lock the legs so standing costs almost nothing. But dreaming comes with a temporary loss of muscle tone — so for REM, the horse must risk lying down.

text: The falling sensation that jolts you awake at the edge of sleep has a name, and about seventy percent of people get it.
caption:
One theory: as muscle tone drops away, a half-asleep brain briefly reads the change as actually falling, and catches you.

getlullable.com

text: Everyone dreams. Most of it is gone within five minutes of waking, and nearly all of it within ten.
attrib: People who say they don't dream simply don't recall
caption:
Wake someone during REM and they'll report a dream almost every time — including people certain they never have any.

text: Sleeping on a problem is not a figure of speech. People who sleep between attempts are about twice as likely to spot the trick.
caption:
Volunteers were given a number puzzle with a hidden shortcut. Those who slept between sessions found it at roughly twice the rate of those who stayed awake the same hours.

text: The record for staying awake on purpose is eleven days. It was set in 1964 by a seventeen-year-old for a science fair.
caption:
By day four he was having trouble with words and faces. He slept fourteen hours afterward, and no one has been encouraged to try it since.

text: Teenagers are not lazy at 7am. Their body clocks genuinely run later, and shift back in their twenties.
caption:
The shift is measurable, near-universal, and reverses on its own with age. School timetables are the part that doesn't move.

getlullable.com

text: Romans divided the night into four watches. Nobody expected to sleep straight through it — the night had structure, like a working day.
caption:
Continuous eight-hour sleep is a young idea. For most of history, night was a place you moved through in stages.

text: People who are totally blind often live on a twenty-five hour day, their sleep drifting later and later around the calendar.
caption:
Without light reaching the clock, it free-runs at its own natural length. It's the clearest evidence of what the internal clock does when the sun stops correcting it.

text: Twice a minute, in light sleep, your brain fires a half-second burst of activity. They're called spindles, and they sort the day.
caption:
Spindle activity tracks with what's remembered the next morning. Some of the night's most useful work happens in the stage people dismiss as shallow.

getlullable.com

text: During deep sleep, the space between brain cells widens, and fluid moves through more freely.
caption:
The channels open when you go under and narrow when you wake. Rest turns out to be a physical process, not just an absence of activity.

text: A house cat sleeps twelve to sixteen hours a day and is, by any measure available, doing better than you.
caption:
Roughly two-thirds of a cat's life is spent asleep. It has never once been asked to justify this.

text: A common swift can stay in the air for ten months without landing once. It sleeps on the wing.
caption:
Some individuals never touched down for the entire non-breeding season. Whatever sleep is for, it can apparently be done at altitude, in motion.

getlullable.com

text: Sleep isn't one long state. It's four or five cycles of about ninety minutes, and the last ones are almost entirely dreaming.
caption:
This is why the final hours matter more than they feel like they should — cut them short and you lose REM disproportionately.

getlullable.com

text: A desert snail can sleep for three years, sealed inside its own shell, waiting for rain.
caption:
One museum specimen, glued to a display card and assumed dead for four years, revived when it was placed in water.

getlullable.com

text: You are at your coldest, and your least alert, about two hours before you normally wake up.
caption:
It's why 4am feels the way it does. The body is at the bottom of its own curve, and will climb out on its own.

text: Ducks sleeping in a row will keep one eye open — but only the ones on the ends, facing out.
attrib: The birds in the middle sleep with both closed
caption:
The outer birds spend more time in single-hemisphere sleep, and turn to point the open eye away from the group. Vigilance is distributed by position.

getlullable.com

text: The best thing to fall asleep to is something interesting enough to follow, and not interesting enough to finish.
caption:
A mind handed nothing to do will find something — usually tomorrow. The trick isn't emptiness, it's a gentle occupation.

text: Sleep that knits up the ravelled sleave of care.
caption:
A sleave was a tangle of unspun silk. Four hundred years on, nobody has improved on the image.

text: Blessings on him who invented sleep, the mantle that covers all human thoughts.
caption:
Sancho Panza, who is the only character in the book with any sense about rest.

text: Even a soul submerged in sleep is hard at work, and helps make something of the world.
caption:
Written roughly twenty-four centuries before anyone could measure what a sleeping brain does. He was right anyway.

getlullable.com

text: Come, blessed barrier between day and day.
caption:
From a sonnet written by a man who could not sleep, addressed to sleep, complaining about it. The insomnia poem is its own small genre.

text: Rest is not idleness, and to lie sometimes on the grass under the trees is by no means a waste of time.
caption:
Written the same decade the electric light started shortening everyone's night. He saw where it was going.

getlullable.com

text: Sleep is the golden chain that ties health and our bodies together.
caption:
A playwright in plague-era London, who spent seven years in debtors' prison and presumably knew something about bad nights.

text: There is a time for many words, and there is also a time for sleep.
caption:
Odysseus, halfway through telling the longest story in Western literature, stopping himself.

getlullable.com

text: In our sleep, pain that cannot forget falls drop by drop upon the heart.
caption:
The oldest surviving description of the thing that wakes you at 3am.
